content: 1. Health facilities should encourage postpartum women to undergo medical assessments at maternal and child health facilities as soon as possible after delivery. This ensures the initiation or continuation of appropriate HIV interventions. 2. Follow-up care, linkage to treatment, and postpartum care are particularly critical for women living with HIV and their HIV-exposed infants. 3. The initial care for HIV-exposed infants is typically scheduled during their first immunization visit, which occurs between four to six weeks of age. This visit includes reinforcement of safe feeding practices, a review of antiretroviral (ARV) coverage, and early infant diagnostic testing for HIV. 4. Ideally, follow-up care for the mother should be scheduled at the same time as the infant’s visit. This care should include a postpartum health check, family planning counseling, a review of the mother’s ARV regimen, and adherence support. 5. The recommendation to initiate antiretroviral therapy (ART) in children is conditional due to limited evidence supporting earlier initiation in certain age groups. However, this approach is expected to provide significant programmatic advantages in settings with limited access to immunological testing, high pediatric HIV burden, and low ART coverage among children. 6. Priority for ART initiation should be given to children younger than two years of age, regardless of WHO clinical stage or CD4 cell count, due to their higher risk of mortality. Children aged two to five years with advanced disease (WHO HIV clinical stages 3 and 4) or CD4 counts ≤750 cells/mm³ or <25% should also be prioritized. 7. ART should be initiated in all children under five years of age who are infected with HIV, regardless of WHO clinical stage or CD4 cell count. Infants diagnosed within the first year of life should receive immediate treatment. 8. For children aged five years and older, ART should be initiated if their CD4 cell count is ≤500 cells/mm³, regardless of WHO clinical stage. Priority should be given to those with CD4 counts ≤350 cells/mm³. 9. ART should be initiated in any child younger than 18 months with a presumptive clinical diagnosis of HIV infection, regardless of age or CD4 count. 10. Infants and young children have an exceptionally high risk of poor outcomes from HIV infection. Without intervention, up to 52% of children die before the age of two years. By five years of age, the risk of mortality and disease progression decreases to levels similar to those of young adults. 11. Early infant diagnosis programs have improved the identification of HIV-infected infants, but the initiation of ART for these children remains suboptimal. Many eligible children are not receiving ART, and pediatric ART coverage lags significantly behind adult coverage. 12. Diagnosing and retaining HIV-exposed and HIV-infected children in care is challenging due to their dependence on caregivers. Loss to follow-up is particularly high along the continuum of care, especially for children in HIV care but not yet eligible for ART. 13. Some countries have introduced immediate ART for children younger than five years based on operational and programmatic considerations. This approach simplifies pediatric treatment and facilitates significant expansion of ART coverage for young children. 14. Expanding ART initiation to all children younger than five years eliminates the need for CD4 testing to determine treatment eligibility in this age group. However, baseline CD4 testing remains important for treatment monitoring in the absence of viral load testing. 15. ART regimens for children should prioritize simplified, less toxic, and more convenient options, such as fixed-dose combinations. For children older than three years, once-daily regimens with a non-thymidine NRTI backbone (e.g., TDF + FTC or TDF + 3TC) and one NNRTI (e.g., EFV) are preferred. 16. The use of d4T in first-line ART regimens should be discontinued due to its well-documented metabolic toxicities. It should only be used in special cases where other ARV drugs are unavailable and for the shortest duration possible. 17. For children co-infected with HIV and HBV, the natural history of the disease is poorly understood, and the benefits of earlier ART initiation remain to be assessed. However, ART regimens should consider the dual management of both infections. 18. Expanding ART services requires ensuring retention in care and supporting adherence. This is particularly important for children younger than two years, who are at higher risk of rapid disease progression and mortality. 19. More research is needed to assess the clinical benefits of early ART initiation in children younger than five years, including its impact on morbidity, immunological response, and virological outcomes over time. 20. National programs should determine the best strategies for implementing universal ART for children younger than five years, balancing operational feasibility with clinical and immunological criteria for older children.
